utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday, 29th of September, 2008. Good afternoon to the accused, the Defence counsel, Mr. Scott and his team, and all the people helping us out. Today we're going to have a witness. He is going to come in a minute, but before he does I will give the floor to the registrar because he had a few IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Kozulj, Ilija. The list submitted I 1D shall be given IC 00856. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00857, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit number IC 00858. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kovacic, I believe you wanted to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for having given me the floor. Good afternoon to Your Honours. Good afternoon to all in the courtroom. Your Honours, I would like to seek permission to file a response, namely on the 11th of September, the Defence teams of General Praljak and General Petkovic filed a motion to review the Trial Chamber decision of the 4th of September. This decision regulated the right of the OTP for additional examination of Defence witnesses. This examination would deal with subjects that were not dealt with in the direct examination. Actually, it is an interpretation of Rule 90(H). On the 25th of September, the OTP responded in writing, and after we looked at the response, the Defence teams of Generals Praljak and Petkovic prepared a brief response to the response filed by the Prosecutor. We believe that a response is needed, especially in view of the argumentation that should be put forth with regard to a few questions that were dealt with in the response of the Prosecution. Therefore, we ask the Honourable Trial Chamber to allow us to act accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, after discussing the matter, the Trial Chamber gives you leave to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to the schedule. We are sitting today, and we'll be sitting on Wednesday. On Wednesday, exceptionally so, we shall finish at 20 past 1.00, not as usual as quarter to 2.00 but at 20 past 1.00 because the Judges are to meet with personalities, VIP, from the Security Council. This is the reason why we shall finish at 20 past 1.00. With regard to the witness today, Mr. Karnavas, how many hours are you planning for your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. We had scheduled the gentleman for three hours. We will endeavour to do our direct testimony in less than that. Now, if I say two hours then you're going to hold me to it, so that's why I'm not giving you an exact figure, but I hope within two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfect. Let's have the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I hope the interpretation is working okay. Can you please give me your first name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm Miroslav Palameta. I was born on the 1st of November, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a current occupation? If so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a university professor, a full professor at the university of Split and the university of Mostar, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, have you had an opportunity to testify before a court of law, be it international or national, or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, this is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, some information. You are a Defence witness. You have been called by the Prlic Defence, and I suppose that prior to coming here you met with Mr. Karnavas as part of the proofing for your testimony. Therefore, you will initially answer questions put to you by Mr. Karnavas, and he may have some documents to submit to you. Following this initial stage, the Prosecutor, you can see two people but only one is going to ask you questions as part of cross-examination. It also is possible for other Defence counsel, since there are six accused in this trial, but for Mr. Prlic there will be another five Defence teams, they, too, might put questions to you as part of their cross-examination. You have three Judges. Usually there are four of us but one of us is absent. These three Judges will also have questions for you at any time. Usually we make an effort -- sometimes we do ask questions when there is a document being shown to you, but afterwards, depending on the momentum and on the situation or based on the document we'll have questions, especially if the document is part of a binder with tens and scores of documents. So then we decide to ask you straight away, but in theory it would be better if the Judges had their questions after the parties have examined you, but it is on a case-by-case basis. Do endeavour to provide specific answers, but you are a university professor. Therefore, I have no fear in this respect. If you fail to understand the meaning of a question, do not hesitate to ask for clarification. And even if a Judge were to put a question in awkward fashion, do not hesitate to ask him to reformulate because Judges are not perfect. They're not infallible either. We have breaks every hour and a half. We break then for 20 minutes. You have read out the solemn declaration. Therefore, from now on you are a witness of justice, of the court. You will therefore have no further contacts with Mr. Karnavas until the end of your testimony. You should finish on Thursday. Since tomorrow is a UN holiday, we will not be sitting tomorrow. You will have to stay in The Hague, but it is a very pleasant city, so I'm sure that you will be happy to have a bit of a day off tomorrow. So without further ado, let me greet Mr. Karnavas again, and I'll ask him to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Palameta, if you could begin by telling us a little bit about your background, your educational background. We can go rather quickly. I do understand that you began with your first degree in -- in Zagreb, at the University of Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, tell us what did you study, and briefly tell us the rest of your educational background.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In 1972, I got my degree from the faculty of philosophy in Zagreb. My major was in the Yugoslav languages and literature and Latin language and literature as my minor. After that I went to Herzegovina, and I worked at a secondary school in Stolac, Capljina, Ljubusko, Ljubinje. All of these are small towns on the east and -- to the east and west of Neretva. In 1981, I got my Masters Degree in the field of Philology. Then I applied for a doctorate at the university in Zagreb and then I transferred to the university in Sarajevo; and in 1984 I got my doctorate again in the field of philology throughout this time, I worked at the secondary school in Stolac and then in 1989, I started working at the school of pedagogy in Mostar and after of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. First, you don't need to lean forward, otherwise you're going to be very tired by the end of the evening. So you can lean back. The mics can pick you up, but you may have to speak a little louder. Secondly, if you want the chair raised, we can raise that because I know you are a big man. You can be assisted. Do you want it raised or are you comfortable where you are?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thirdly, everything is being translated. Now, I know that you're very eloquent, but you're going to need to speak a little slow so as to not tire out those who are translating you, okay?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we were at 19 -- 1989. So pick it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In 1989, I started working at the academy of pedagogy in Mostar. After the first multi-party elections, I was offered a position at the republican Ministry of Education in Sarajevo. I worked there for about a year from 1981 until 1982 as under-secretary. That is the third-ranking official in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this would be 1991 until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes. 1991 until April 1992. As I lived in Stolac with my family, every Friday I would go home for the weekend and then I'd leave on Sunday. Then I could no longer return. That is to say I could not go to Sarajevo, because at the time there were no communications, so I stayed in Stolac. I stayed with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, what month are we speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The very beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we continue with the story, let's back up a little bit. First you told us that at one point you were in Mostar working at the academy there. Please tell us exactly what you were teaching.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I taught the methodology of teaching languages and literature. At that time the language involved was called Serbo-Croat or Croato-Serbian. That was the subject that I taught. In actual fact, it has to do with how you teach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And before that, if you could tell us what sort of courses you taught.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Before that I worked at a secondary school, and I taught Latin. I also taught literature and the Croato-Serbian or Serbo-Croat language. That is what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Officially, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We got that part. When you were teaching I take it you -- when you were teaching Serbian Croatian or Croatian Serbian you were teaching grammar, orthography, that's what you were --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. When you went to the Ministry of education and you were the deputy secretary, I believe, is that what you said that you were?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I was the under-secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what exactly were you doing as the under-secretary for the Ministry of Education in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: As for these administrative affairs, the position of the under-secretary in the ministry meant that he was actually head of the ministry itself. He took part in certain meetings that have to do with preparing bills that are then translated by lawyers into the language of law, responding to issues that crop up in the field and things like that. However, it was also possible to be on certain commissions. That depended on the government itself who would be appointed as member of a particular commission. That would basically be the work involved. Since this government was conceived on the basis of a principle of equal representation of ethnic groups, as a representative of Croat interests I raised questions if I believed that Croatian interests were not being put forth properly. That is also what was done by the Serb representative and the Muslim representative was actually the minister himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Concretely -- and again you don't need to lean forward. Sit back and relax or you're going to get tired. Just speak a little louder or move the mics a bit forward. Now, were you involved in any commissions at that time, and if so, could you tell us concretely what exactly you were involved in? What sort of subjects were --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I remember that at that time, I think it was in 1991, I was a member of a commission that was supposed to examine the situation in Herzegovina, because already by then some things were happening on the ground that were a threat to law and order. Certain incidents occurred. Krajinas were being established, and we needed to send a commission to the area to see what was going on. There was a Serb representative, a Muslim representative, and I was there on that commission. We attended different meetings out in the field. The report we compiled we actually never submitted because it was not topical as a war broke out. The actual state of war broke out. So this was this other commission that I worked on briefly, namely the commission on language, the constitutional commission that was supposed to provide proposals as to how to resolve in the constitution the name of the language of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So this issue came up as early as 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: It could have been at the very end. I don't remember exactly whether it was the beginning or -- no, it was the end of 1991. A meeting was held, and on behalf of the cultural societies that existed then representing the culture and interests of respective ethnic groups, Alija Isakovic was there, then Professor Kovacevic on behalf of Prosveta, the Serb society; and I was there on behalf of Napredak, the Croatian society, and we discussed certain issues related to naming the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Hold on. We're going to go step-by-step. You mentioned two individuals, that they were there on behalf of the Serb society; is that correct? Or was one of them on behalf of the Muslims, or there was no Muslim representative?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I do apologise. Alija Isakovic was there on behalf of Preporod, the Muslim society. Professor Kovacevic represented Prosveta, the Serb so the. I was there Miroslav Palameta on behalf of Napredak, the Croat cultural society. So what was discussed was the name of the language as it would be stipulated in the new constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Karnavas. I would like only to ask Professor Palameta if you would kindly tell us the equivalent of those three names, that is the Prosveta and also the Napredak, I believe, and the third one was the Muslim paper. It is not Napredak. Do I not find it. But anyway if you tell me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Preporod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: So then the English equivalent I mean after translation of those three societies, if you would be able to repeat again the three names. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Preporod.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Renaissance, renewal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was for whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Then Napredak, the -- well, Preporod was the Muslim cultural society.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Napredak, which is "progress." That was the Croat society. Prosveta, well, that's a well-known thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters notes education, enlightenment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We don't know it that's why we're asking.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's okay Judge Prandler? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And these societies existed prior to the election?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, these societies existed for a long time. They had been in existence for a long time; however, sometime in 1948 and 1949 they stopped operating or perhaps even before that. Then they were reactivated in the beginning of the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need to go through the historical part of that. If you could just tell us now, because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, there is a great deal of background note and we cannot hear the speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be fair when we are talking about the names of the respective society Napredak was not the name of the society. It was the Croatian cultural society of Napredak is the full name and that would be right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. The gentleman who intervened is quite right. The Croatian cultural society Napredak, the Serb Cultural Society Prosveta, and the Muslim Cultural Society Preporod. I do apologise for not having provided the full names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now that we have the full names and we know what they mean, perhaps you could tell us concretely what exactly were the issues. You said that what -- you talked about the constitution and the language. What exactly was the issue of the language?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The fundamental issue that had to be resolved was the name of the language. The old model which was the constitutional solution previously, i.e., Croato-Serbian or Serbo-Croatian was considered to be exhausted, spent, and a new name had to be provided. The proposal of the Croatian cultural society, Napredak was that the language be called Croatian in the constitution. The proposal of the Serb cultural society Prosveta or rather Professor Kovacevic was that the language be called the Serbian language. At that point in time, Mr. Alija Isakovic did not express his opinion on how the language should be called, on what it should be called. He said that everybody had the right to call his or her own language by the name of the people they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Well, that's what I said," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I mentioned all three ethnic groups, and I mentioned the name of the language -- or, rather, I said the Croats will probably call their language Croatian, the Serbs will call their language Serbian, and the Muslims can call theirs whatever they like. But Professor Kovacevic said I was not speaking on behalf of anybody but the cultural society Napredak and that this was a moot point. I am not a linguist, and I could not speak on behalf of others. There was somebody there whose job this was. I listened to radio broadcasts at the time and there was a professor, Musamir Reuzic [phoen], a very eminent and renowned professor from the faculty of philosophy who said in a radio broadcast dedicated to this constitutional issues and issues of language that the language should be called Bosnian Croatian Serbian in various combinations with the words in different order, but this had not been decided yet. It was still a public debate which was ongoing and no name had as yet been determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right here because in the transcript it says that he, meaning Alija Isakovic, was the with one that had made the proposal of each nation having the language called after their nation, and then if we listened on --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No. I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, if we could continue at this point. So was that proposal that you -- the one that you had heard over the radio, was that something that was discussed? Was it adopted? Okay. Let me ask that question again. You indicated that you had heard a very prominent member make a proposal as to what the language should be called and my question was was that proposal discussed? Yes, no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a radio broadcast, and the professor spoke on this broadcast in Radio Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I'm saying in the commission, did the commissioners discuss it, you and the others?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I did not engage in this debate further. I thought that professors of language would be more competent to discuss this issue, because after this intervention of mine which was perceived as incorrect, I adopted a low profile in this respect, and then Professor Kovacevic continued the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here then. Well, did the -- did anyone from the Muslims come up with a proposal as to what they wanted their language to be called? I know that there was a society of Muslim intellectuals. That's what they called themselves. Did they or any other society of Muslims come -- come up with any proposals as to what the language could or should be called?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes. This was in 1992, in the autumn of 1992, actually -- or, rather, in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm speaking about the commission, the commission that you're in.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In this commission I never heard anybody say that the language could be called by a third name. We had only two meetings, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the issue ever resolved?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Not by this commission, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did the commission ever issue a report on its discussions with respect to what language should be adopted in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The commission did not continue to meet, because as early as January, the Serbs adopted their own constitution. This was in 1992. And in this constitution they called their language the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's pick up, then, from April 1992 you indicated that you had gone -- that on the weekends you would go back to Stolac and at some point in early April 1992 you were unable to go back. Could you please explain -- that is from Stolac back to Sarajevo. Could you please explain why you were unable to go back?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: All links with Sarajevo had been cut off. Sarajevo was encircled, and it was simply not possible to return there. It was also very difficult to leave Sarajevo. I remember that Minister Hasic, who was the minister at the time, called me up in Stolac asking me if I could escort his wife who wanted to go towards Split and then on to some European country. There was already this problem in Sarajevo that one could not leave or return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- so what did you do? And we need to move quickly because that's not the real essence of the testimony. So what did you after in April 1992? You couldn't go back to Sarajevo. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I remained in Stolac, and then I was called from the Crisis Staff of the HVO. They asked me to join them, so I did. Around the 10th, there was already an attack on Stolac -- or, rather, the units of the Yugoslav army --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In what month?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: -- and the irregular Serb forces entered Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Palameta, I'm going to have to caution you as I did during the proofing session that we need to be as precise as we can with times. So when you say the 10th, we weren't around Stolac on the 10th whatever month it was and whatever year. So you need to be precise. Was it the 10th of May, June, July? What month are we talking about and what year?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: It was the 10th of April, 1992. The units of the Yugoslav army and the Serb irregular forces entered Stolac on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: After this it was agreed in the Crisis Staff that the population should be evacuated quickly, that portion of the population which was not able to fight, that some sort of resistance should be mounted if necessary, and in accordance with this men were stationed with weapons in certain places near settlements. However, when the women, children, and the elderly had already crossed the river Neretva, and they did that in Pocitelj, the HVO units simply melted from the field, and this happened over a period of over two or three days. And I left at that time, likewise. In the area of Neum, Metkovic, and the Croatian Primorje area where refugees were accommodated several of us from the Crisis Staff worked on providing accommodation for these people and endeavouring to prepare the existing units so that they could return to Stolac when the time came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, one minor question on my part. You explained that the Serbs entered Stolac on the 10th of April, 1992, and that at the level of the Crisis Staff you did what was necessary. I'm interested in the following because this is at the very heart of the Trial Chamber's concerns. This Stolac municipality, did you of your own accord react to the events, or did you receive instructions from somewhere else? Was your Crisis Staff a Crisis Staff that took actions in view of the situation that necessitated a reaction because the Serbs were entering Stolac, or did you act on instructions from outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge there were no instructions coming from outside. At that point in time, we had to respond to the situation. Nobody expected that the Serb units would pass through Stolac. That was my impression. That's what I know from that time. There was an agreement between the Croatian and Muslim side that this would not be allowed. However, people did expect something similar to happen because in the area, as far as I know, there was already a build-up of the forces of the Uzice and Titograd Corps. They were in Berkovici, in Stolac municipality, and in neighbouring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to go into detail, but you just mentioned something. You said that the reactions came from the Croats and the Muslims. This means that in Stolac, in April 1992, there was a bloc made of Croats and Muslims against the Serbs. Was it so?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: That bloc was something that didn't actually exist. There was just the idea that joint resistance should be mounted, but it never actually materialised at any point. All these ideas were put aside by the Muslims as far as I know, but I was not personally involved in those agreements. I was just told that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for all this. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor, and I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, a couple of points to follow up. What did you do exactly in the Crisis Staff, and number two, how long were you in there? In other words, give us the period, from this month to that month, or this month to that year.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: This was from April until my return in the summer of that same year. We returned to Stolac in June, the 13th of June that is. The same year, yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you remain working with the Crisis Staff after June 13th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I did not work in the Crisis Staff, in fact, but instead there was a form of social or community work in which my colleagues, Muslims and Croats, participated dealing with certain issues of humanitarian aid. These were issues not linked to wartime activities but, rather, to an attempt to normalise life, because the refugees had started to return from the seaside and from the places where they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did the -- did the Muslims return as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: When refugees were leaving Stolac there weren't many Muslims among them. When the Croats left, I remember there was an agreement that the Muslims should also be invited. The Muslim neighbours should be told that the Croats were leaving, and if they wanted to come along they could, and many did. But if Pocitelj, there was a SDA organisation. Pocitelj is a town on the river Drina, and the Muslims were told that they should not go any further but that they should return to their homes. So at that point in time there were no Muslims returning from the seaside except for perhaps just a few, a small number. I can't tell you what the number was precisely, but it was mostly Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when exactly did you stop working with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In the course of the summer of 1992 I stopped working in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: After that I mostly devoted myself to my work at the university, because as early of June after Mostar was liberated, in June 1992, there was a meeting at the university on how the next academic year should be organised, the teaching, the examinations, which were to be organised in Siroki Brijeg and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how did that go? How successful were you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Well, we did as well as could be expected under the circumstances. You couldn't really work in Mostar because there was constant shelling from the surrounding hills and from the positions held by the Serbian army, and for this reason examinations and lectures and classes were organised in Siroki Brijeg, a place which is about 20 kilometres away from Mostar. And under the circumstances, we did quite well. The professors who had to go from Mostar would take a car or a bus every day and return in the after noon. Also, the students who had to go to Siroki Brijeg from Mostar did the same. And the other students who could come from the free areas and areas where there was no combat, they would gather in Siroki Brijeg in an area -- or, rather, in a building which was actually the building -- the club of the Croatian cultural society Napredak. Then it became a students' dormitory, and then when the war broke out, Napredak prepared this building as a sort of lecture theatre. Of course it wasn't really an ideal place for academic work, and the town itself couldn't provide the students with everything they needed, accommodation, a library, and so on, and it couldn't provide their teachers with that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go step-by-step here. I'd prefer if you would just give us shorter answers to my questions and I'll try to keep my questions rather narrow. Now, we do -- we've heard testimony that the name was changed, the name of the university was changed. Do you recall what the name was changed from to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The university in Mostar used to be called the Dzemal Bijedic University. This was the name of a politician. And I remember that even before the war there were many initiatives to have the name changed, because Dzemal Bijedic, although he was a nice man, a pleasant man, was not really an intellectual. He had never written a book. So even before the war there was this idea that the name of the university should be changed. So now the name was changed. To the best of my recollection, the commission included the general secretary and three professors, two Muslims and two Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: And this was declared on the 25th as the new name of the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what was the name of the university then? What was it changed to? What was my original question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: It was called the Mostar University -- or, rather, the University in Mostar. That was its new name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And in order for us to move along rather quickly, you know, when I ask you what, it's okay if you just give me the what part of the answer. Then I'll follow up with a why so I can have the explanation. That would -- we can move rather quicker that way. Now, language. We heard testimony that the language was changed, the use of the language was changed in the university as well as in schools, and it was now the language of Croatian. Is that correct and, if so, why did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This happened for a very simple reason. During the war the name of the language, Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian, caused revulsion among people because this part of this name, Serb, was the name of the enemy in war. In January 1992, the Republika Srpska in its constitution omitted the Croat component from the name, and they called their language Serbian. So for this reason the Croats called their language Croatian. They simply deleted that part of the name which mentioned Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, again I'm going to take this step-by-step because this is very critical. So my first question regarding this is: When the name was changed, did -- were any efforts made to import a new language called Croatian? In other words, what was being taught in Croatian, assuming it was a separate language, and I'm not suggesting that it was not, were efforts made to now bring in a new language with new textbooks regarding grammar, orthography, a dictionary, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. My next question then is: Was there a reaction, to your knowledge, by the Muslims at the time, because before the change of the language there was Serbo-Croatian or Croatian-Serbian, now it's called Croatian, did they object to the change of the language and, if so, could you please describe to us to what extent you're aware of any objections raised by Muslims and by whom in the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Allow me to add something to my response to your previous question, because perhaps it's not clear to our audience. The issue of naming the language as Serbian or Croatian is something that existed in the constitution of 1946. Not just the constitution of Yugoslavia but also that of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The name was changed, so in 1974 it was changed to Croato-Serbian or Serbo-Croatian, but the name Croatian already existed, as did the name Serbian in the first constitution after World War II in socialist Yugoslavia. This is another element indicating that the name was not imported. The name simply fluctuated in the area itself. As regards your question about whether I heard any reactions, no, I didn't hear of any reactions to that issue -- or, rather, to the introduction of the name of the Croatian language. The first time I heard a reaction to that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's talk about that then. When was it in 1993, and how did you -- how was this reaction expressed to you, if it was expressed directly to you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: After the summer of 1992, I was invited to the newly established office for education in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as the deputy head, and I did both jobs at that time. I continued to teach at the university as well. Sometime in March, towards the end of March 1993 or perhaps in early April, I'm not sure of the exact date, I was invited to go to Mr. Jadranko Prlic's office, and then Mr. Prlic himself spoke on the phone, and he said that some Muslims from Mostar had arrived in his office. It was a delegation headed by Mr. Jahic, and they had an objection to the school curriculum, and he said that this delegation would be coming to see us, to explain to us what their objections were. On that occasion Mr. Prlic asked us to try to find the best possible solution to this problem. About half an hour later, Mr. Jahic arrived with three or four other people. I don't know their names, and they didn't say much. Mr. Jahic said he had a major objection, because in the curriculum for literature there were no Muslim writers, and Muslim writers should be included in the curriculum. I replied that this problem could easily be resolved, that they should simply deliver to us a list of the names of authors and the names of literary works to be incorporated into the curriculum and that could be the end of this discussion. After this I consulted -- or, rather, he consulted the people who were with him - I don't know what they were saying - and he said there was another problem, that Muslims could not study the Croatian language in school. I replied that this was a problem that I personally could not resolve at that point in time. The -- it's one thing to change the name of a subject and another to intervene in the programme, but that he as a high-ranking official in his own party could initiate a discussion with the partner party, the HDZ or the HVO, and offer to them a solution whereby the name they chose for the language could be used in those schools where there was Muslim population; or the name could change depending on the school population. And we agreed that those persons who were in charge of developing the curricula, and those were the people in the institute for language and literature, should discuss this and come up with the list. That is to say that a few days later this meeting did take place. However, the list that we had discussed was not submitted. One of the members of the delegation presented the entire curriculum for secondary schools that was supposed to be changed in actual fact, the entire curriculum. I found it a bit strange that there was no mention of what we had discussed earlier on. At that meeting, of course, it wasn't language that was discussed. What were discussed were other suggests, history and geography namely. Then we called in people who dealt with that. However, there was no positive outcome of this meeting, and my impression was at that time that actually a solution was not being sought. The things that happened after that proved me right. Actually, in that area, that is to say Mostar and further to the south, clashes started between the BH army and the HVO. So the well-known developments of Mostar started taking place. Offices were moved from the front line where it was dangerous to be. That is what I recall. That is what I recall now. That is what was brought up during this discussion on language and literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me go back and clarify some points, again step-by-step. So there's no need to give lengthy answers at this point. First of all, when did the school year begin? I mean, you told us when this meeting took place, late March, early -- late March, early April 1992, but when had the school year begun that year?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I think that the school year, as far as I can remember, in 1993 was supposed to start only sometime in the month of April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you missed my point. There was a school -- when they arrived, the school year for 1992/1993 was ongoing; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes. In those localities that were not areas where there was military engagement. I think that at that point in Mostar there wasn't anything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You really have to help us out here though. When had the school year begun, because you're saying that they came towards the end of the school year, if the next school year, 1993/1994 is about to start sometime in April, but when did it start?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: It started in the autumn. It's supposed to start in September, and that's when it started in those localities where there were no military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: September what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the proposal now that they were making, late March, early April, was that an entire curriculum for the 1993 to 1994 school year or for the one that was ongoing and was about to finish? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: It was the curriculum that included all years. That is to say that it was the general curriculum that cannot be adopted within a short span of time. That was the problem that related to years 1, 3, and 4. The proposal did not state for what year it was, and it wasn't stated that it was for the year to come. It was supposed to be incorporated straight away in the existing school year, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what would -- what would the problem have been to, say, have this curriculum for the 1993/1994? 1992/1993, we understand that year's almost over, but why not take that curriculum that they were proposing and maybe work with that for the following year, that is the following academic year from 1993 to 1994? What was the problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Actually, that curriculum was one that I had devised myself a few years before that for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was a proposal for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it meant that schools in -- that schools in Republika Srpska were supposed to work on the basis of that curriculum, that is to say including Serb, Muslim, and Croat children. So the content was quite different than it would be at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Palameta, maybe we're not -- we're missing something in translation. The Muslims are dissatisfied. They come with -- they complain that they're not teaching any of the Muslim writers. Okay. Then they propose a curriculum. You say it was unrealistic. Now I'm asking you to explain to us how it would be unrealistic for you to adopt that curriculum for the 1993 to 1994 year. What made it unrealistic in your -- in your eyes? That's what I'm asking. Be as specific and as concrete.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: That curriculum was not acceptable in that situation. It still included some things that we might term ideological. Also, the curriculum included some things that were there as a compromise. As I've already mentioned, Serbian writers were included, although they didn't have to be there, although some actually were there. In this curriculum there weren't any more Muslim writers, but we had agreed that the delegation would bring a proposal of literary works and authors that should be included in the already existing curriculum. Another matter now. There was no insistence whatsoever on resolving the situation at that very moment. I was just an observer. I was just observing the discussion that took place among the people who were in charge of these particular subjects. I did not get the impression that they did want to reach a final agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the issue of language? Did that issue come up, and were any proposals made at that time as to what their language -- what their language should be called?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: At that moment there was no mention whatsoever of language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me go back a little bit. You indicated that you were deputy head for the office of -- on education. Who was the head, the head of office?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Professor Hasic was -- no, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. You're talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: So it was Minister Hasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Actually, I apologise. I'm speaking -- you indicated that you were the deputy head of the office for education for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I said deputy head. I think I said that, deputy head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that's what I said. I don't know whether it was translated, but when were you deputy head? From when to where -- from when -- from what period did you start and when did you end?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: From the autumn of 1992 all the way up to sometime in 1994 when the Croat community -- or, rather, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna ceased to operate. This was after the Washington accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So did you participate much -- you would have participated in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Were you in one of the ministries at that point?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what position did you hold then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: At the time of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, it was called the head of the office and deputy head of the office. At the time when the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed then that office was called the ministry, and I was the deputy minister at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just briefly could you please tell us during this period what sort of issues were you involved in as deputy head, deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I personally was also the assistant for higher education. There were people who dealt with elementary education, with secondary education, with culture. The main role of the entire ministry was to confirm certain curricula, to pass certain decisions in the given situation. There was a war going on, and we were functioning in special circumstances. All the decisions that were passed were of a temporary or provisional nature. The key thing was to distribute money, that is to say finance schools and universities, to secure these funds and the allocation of these funds and conditions for teaching as such. These were the main things that we dealt with, myself included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just -- we're going to go through some documents at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I apologise. I see you want to move on to something else, but I have a question. Witness, I'd like to go back to the question of the change in the name of Mostar university. I want to make sure I really understood you well. I note that from the fall of 1992 to 1994 you were deputy head of the national education system as well as professor at Mostar university. Is that it? You were deputy head in charge of education, and you were also a professor. Very well. Thank you. You know -- do you know when the university of Mostar got its name of Dzemal Bijedic? What was it called Dzemal Bijedic University.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly when that happened, but at any rate it is certain that that was the name of the university for ten years before the war started, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. After Mostar was freed, according to my notes, to what I noted down, and what you told us, the university changed its name; and you said that this was motivated by the fact that this Dzemal Bijedic was not really a great writer or a great academic. I'm a bit surprised, because throughout the world there are many names of universities. Sometimes they're called after generals, heads of States, professors, a bit of everything, actually, from every walk of life, and it seems to be the case with this Dzemal Bijedic as the name. And then in 1992 people note that because this person is not an academic and does not have enough publications, the name has to be changed. Was that the only motivation, or do you believe there were other motivations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were other motives involved too. I just mentioned what the reasons why that were being fluctuated by way of responses to the situation. Names of universities and schools were not supposed to be burdened by ideology any longer. For the most part these names had come from a group of names with a strong Communist prefix; that is to say Dzemal Bijedic and other names that were used for naming institutions were for the most part either Communists or Partisans during the Second World War. That is to say Communists yet again. Another thing, by your leave, Your Honour, this had happened at other universities as well throughout the former Yugoslavia. Names were changed that had an ideological dimension belonging to the former system. So that was the case in Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I gave a sufficient explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... also bore the names of Communists, that identified with the previous system?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And I believe Titograd, is that -- did that city get its name from Tito, or did it exist prior to 1945 as Titograd?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Titograd, the capital of Montenegro, used to be called Podgorica, and then after 1945 it was named after Tito. Now it is being fluctuated as Podgorica again. It is called Podgorica. Then in neighbouring Croatia there was the port of Ploce. In Communist times it was called Kardeljevo. It was named after the Communist ideologue, Kardelj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll talk about the change of the names a little bit later more concretely, but I want to move on at least very quickly before the break and finish with your background. After you left being the deputy minister in the Ministry of Education, what did you do? That would have been 1994, I believe. Just very briefly if you could tell us your background thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: After 1994, I worked as a professor only at the faculty of pedagogy in Mostar, because in the meantime the academy of pedagogy was formed into a faculty of pedagogy. I worked there. After that and after the Dayton Accords, I was a member of the Dayton Commission for National Monuments. And at the moment when diplomacy was being discussed, I was also put forth as a candidate for an ambassador in some country. The country involved was Italy. I accepted that, and I spent almost four years there as the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then I went back to university, because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you. Let me stop you here. Again, it's critical that we have these dates, these years. You have to work with me, Mr. Palameta. You have to work with me on the dates. From what time? When were you appointed, and when were you relieved of your ambassadorship in Italy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I would have to remember very specifically, because I must say as far as accurate dates are concerned, I simply cannot operate with that kind of thing. I have to try to remember now. Now, I think it was in 2007 that I was appointed, in the autumn. I am sorry. I am sorry. It was 1997. That's what I meant. And then I went to Italy in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And how long did you stay in Italy? When did you return?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I stayed there for almost four years. That is to say three years and a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when did you return, sir? What months and what year? That would be 2002 sometime?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No. No. I think it was 2001. The autumn of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then you went back to teaching, and did you take up another post at some point?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was to the Vatican; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Not at that point in time. I worked as a professor, but then they made an offer to me yet again to go into the diplomatic yet again, this time to the Vatican. That is to say to be the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Holy See. This was in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How long --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Three years and about eight months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, from when to when? About. Give me a season. A season in the year would do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: All right. It was on the 13th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Until?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Until 1st of November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So those would be complete mandates, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. It's very timely. Mr. Karnavas, you've used up an hour so far, for your information. We will now have a 20-minute break, so let's adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Palameta, we're going to go through some documents and I believe there's a binder for you. I'm sure the Trial Chamber as well as everyone else will be relieved we don't have too many documents. So we'll try to go through these rather quickly. The first document is P 00312, and that should be the first document in your binder. If you look at it, it's titled "Report."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 4 to 12 July, 1992. It looks like a presidential transcript, in fact. And have you had a chance to see this particular document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look on page 5 in the English version, we see your name there, and where you make a few comments. Now, have you had a chance to look at -- to read this report, to actually read it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it. I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you recall being at that meeting or meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, according to the Prosecution's theory, in this particular document Franjo Tudjman is expressing the territorial ambitions of Croatia to regain its historical boundaries and is also involved in organising and establishing the government of the Croatian Defence Council. That's their position. That's how they interpret this document. If you could please tell us to your understanding what was this meeting about and to what extent were you participating in this particular meeting, and please be brief.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: At this time. In the summer of 1992. Several ministers from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina who are mentioned here were on the free territory; and they represented themselves as the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the free territory. I was the third-ranking man in the ministry. I wasn't that important, but I was with them, and at that time certain things had to be done for Sarajevo, which was encircled, and particular ministers had particular tasks in this respect. There followed a visit to Zagreb, Ljubljana, Split, and as you can see from this transcript, the tasks mentioned here concerning Bosnia-Herzegovina such as, for example, opening an office in Zagreb, which was opened and which became the first embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a neighbouring state, this was in fact the only possible exit from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the only place we could go and ask for assistance. I think this is a presidential transcript, in fact, and as we can see here the delegation met inter alia the then-president of Croatia, Tudjman. The conversation held in Vila Zagorje was a conversation which I and others perceived as a discussion, an exchange of information, not any sort of instruction-giving; and there was nothing in these comments. And I discussed this afterwards with my colleagues. There was nothing in this discussion, in President Tudjman's office except for things happening on the ground and certain problems that had arisen. And I should mention that most of these people were members of the HDZ, which only three months previously, before the outbreak of war, had been part of the same party in the former Yugoslavia. For this reason some party issues were discussed. This was just after the war had broken out. Soon after that, I don't know when exactly because I wasn't a party man, there was a separate party established for Bosnia-Herzegovina, a separate HDZ party. We all saw this discussion and perceived it as a situation in which information was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, speaking of the HDZ, have you ever been a member of the of HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we see from this particular discussion that it took place in July 1992. So keeping -- keeping in mind what the Prosecution indicates or how they perceive this meeting to have occurred, let's focus on the next document, 1D 02149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, Witness, I have a couple questions to ask you. Do you remember this meeting with Mr. Tudjman which occurred after an official visit made by a number of officials who met with Mr. Tudjman? Obviously you do remember this meeting, but I have a technical meeting about it. When you met with President Tudjman, were you standing up or were you sitting around the table, you know, sitting around a table, and was there your name on the place where you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were sitting around a table. There were no nameplates, no designated seats. The person who brought the delegation in simply said, "Please take a seat round the table."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you remember taking the floor? In the English version, page 5, we see your name, and there is something written under your name. So do you remember taking the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, and I'm summing up, that war was not -- war with the Muslims was not necessary, that you would rather be for parliamentary discussions as a solution. So you were in favour of negotiations rather than war. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less, yes. I said something like that. If I may explain the situation and what this looked like. The host gave each guest an opportunity of saying something. I did not expect to take the floor, to be invited to take the floor; so my brief discussion was something that referred to other things that had been said at the meeting, something that I felt should be added. I thought it was just protocol, just common politeness to give everybody a chance to take the floor. I was quite surprised to be invited to take the floor myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So now I come to the crux of my question. At one point in time Mr. Mesic spoke up. You know who Mr. Mesic is, of course. You don't have to look at the document. I will tell you exactly what he said. Mr. Mesic took the floor, and he said that in several places there was no longer any authority, that the HVO had re-established authority in these places where civilian entities had been elected. Then he adds: "We recognise the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you remember Mr. Mesic officially saying that, that he recognised the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for a single moment did any of us doubt that Mesic and the others who were there did not recognise the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croatia had recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina sometime in April, at the very beginning of the recognition of that country. So Mr. Mesic's statement was quite normal. It was quite expected. It was just part of a speech, well, that was understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, other people took the floor after Mr. Mesic and I will skip them, but I will return to what Mr. Tudjman said at one point in time. You were there. You attended this meeting, so maybe you remember this. Mr. Tudjman said, and this is on page 7 in the English version, that: "We need Herceg-Bosna," and he adds: "We do not recognise HOS, the HOS." He says, "They are provocateurs from an independent -- for the Independent State of Croatia and we cannot accept that." Did you hear Mr. Tudjman criticise those who wanted to set up an independent state? Do you remember this accurately? He seems to criticise those who belong to the HOS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I remember that criticism by Mr. Tudjman, and you can see it in this document which is a transcript. I remember that he reacted -- well, his facial expressions and gestures when HOS was mentioned showed his reaction; and what it says here, I understand that criticism of the HOS in this case was based on the fact that the HOS by its appearance, uniforms, conduct, was strongly reminiscent of the World War II Independent State of Croatia; and the units that were and remain unpopular and unacceptable and which the enemies of the new State of Croatia at that time were constantly evoking to obstruct the creation of an independent state in order to create a negative image and with the intention of working against all the ideas of that new state, and that's how I understood President Tudjman's intervention and his reaction. In historical terms, the HOS had certain aspirations to the territory of the World War II Independent State of Croatia, and this referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina also. So, in this case, it was a topical subject for discussion among those present at this meeting. His reaction did not surprise any members of the delegation. It was nothing new or unusual. I think he shared the opinion of all the others in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You answered my question. Thank you. I wanted to ask you whether his reaction led to any surprise or comments, and you just said no. Mr. Karnavas. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, 1D 02149, 2149. That's the second document. We see that it says: "To the participants and organizers of the symposium on historical, cultural and artistic relations between the Muslims and Croats," and we see that it is by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, but we don't see a date, and we don't know who -- what the symposium really is all about and who participated other than Mr. Prlic wanting to thank the participates for the symposium which was called "Return to the origins." So can you -- do you know whether -- do you know anything about the symposium? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us, please, about what time, to your recollection, was this symposium held?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, we -- my colleagues and I always commented on current events, and sometime in August 1992 a symposium under this title was held in Zagreb. It was attended by some professors from Mostar, Mr. Sancevic, who was later the first ambassador of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina; Sefko Omerbasic; the Zagreb mufti. Then there was Sevko Tankovic, who at the time was the president of the SDA in Croatia. And I don't remember all the names. There were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the other persons who attended the gathering, but at any rate that was the title of this gathering that was held in August, and this is what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what, if anything, was discussed at this symposium? What was the purpose of it? I mean, we can see from the letter, but if you can tell us first-hand the extent to which you were -- you know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: This was meant to underline the positive links between the Croats and the Muslims throughout history, the creation of a friendly atmosphere between these two peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- we're going to move on to another topic unless there are any questions from the Bench. We'll go to the next document, and the next topic deals primarily with the issue of language. Keeping in mind what you've already told us during the first session let's look at 1D 00468. 1D 00468. It's dated 24 February, 1993. That is decree. We can see that it's from Sarajevo. A "Decree on defining of revised section of constitution of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And -- do you have it, sir? Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we -- if you go to Article II, we see that Article II states quite clearly that there are three nations in Bosnia, the Serbs the Croats and Muslims. Fan we look at Article IV. It says: "In the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Croatia, i.e., Croatian Serbian language with the 'ije' pronunciation is the official use both in Latin and Cyrillic script." Now, you had indicated that at some point the constitution included Croatian and Serbian as language. That's not reflected in this particular constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, you can't see this here because this is just a copy of the constitutional solutions from 1974. There have been no interventions in the text regardless of the fact that in December immediately prior to this the most prominent professors and writers, mostly Muslims, asked that the name of the language be declared for Muslims to be the Bosniak or Bosnian language. A large number of writers, in fact all the well known names of writers, journalists and public figures signed this demand; and on the 22nd of December, 1992, the Muslim intellectuals who signed themselves as I think the wartime Muslim intellectuals or something like that sent a letter of a similar content, but as you can see no solution was included here but, rather, the solution from the constitution of 1974 has simply been copied into this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at the next document. 3D 00182. And again keeping in mind your earlier testimony when you told us late March, early April 1993 you were approached concerning the curriculum at the -- for the schools, here this letter is dated 8 March 1993. At the bottom we can see the name, "President Zijad Demirovic." Do you know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: At the time I heard about him. He was the president of the regional SDA committee for Bosnia-Herzegovina. His name was Zijad Demirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The regional the president of the SDA regional -- regional SDA committee for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina or just Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Only for Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and we see this is addressed to the Ministry for Science and Education. Have you had a chance to look at this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in looking at the document, what conclusions can you draw?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Looking at this document, one can draw several conclusions. First of all that Zijad Demirovic, on behalf of the most powerful political organisation of the Muslims from Herzegovina considers that the language, which at that point in time was being called Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian as in the old constitution was unsuitable and unacceptable for the Muslims. Secondly, there was a need for this to be changed. Thirdly, in this text he complains to the persons responsible, the persons in the ministry and in politics, because they have not raised this issue since this issue is giving rise to various problems including ethnic intolerance. Likewise, he felt, as did the Muslim intellectuals, that every people has the right to call their language by their own name. This is the usual practice throughout the world. Those are several points that spring to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we look at the next document then, 1D 00469. This is 8 April 1993, which would have been on or about the time of your meeting. Here this is a decree with the force of law on suspending of execution of Article 4 of the constitution, the same article that we just saw, and Article 1 reads: "In the time of war regulation of the Article 4 of the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ... will be suspended of execution." So it seems that there is -- they're amending the constitution. And could you please explain -- how do you interpret Article 1? I know that you're not a lawyer, but how do you interpret this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, I am not a lawyer, and I'm not sure whether those who adopted this decision had the right to do so, but in any case this decision suspends the constitutional provision concerning language in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a vacuum is created in this respect because nothing else is provided to replace it. What had existed before is being suspended and room is being opened up for something that is yet to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document 1D 00470. Now we're in August, so several months later. We have another constitutional amendment. I guess you could call it this. This is, "in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, standard literary language with the 'ije' pronunciation of constituent nations which is an appointed by one of three terms: Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian, will be in official use." Were you aware of this change when it was made back in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't aware of it in this form, not precisely, but I knew that this was happening, that three names had been introduced for the language in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The constitutional provision implies that there is one language bearing three different names. That is in fact the constitution solution to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to make sure that I fully understand this, and I want focus you as far on that period of time. Not today but on that period of time when we have this introduction, assuming that it is correct, constitutional, legal, call it whatever you want, when they say, Now the language will be Bosnian, at that time was this a separate language, a different language with a new grammar, orthography, dictionary, than the one that had been used, say, on the 29th of August, 1993, the day before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge it was only then after this decision was adopted that the standardisation of the Bosniak or Bosnian language began. It was only at this point that books began to be written which are a prerequisite for the beginning of standardisation. I'm referring to the grammar which was published at that time in 1994 and the orthography which was published, the book about orthography which was published at the same time. What I read about this in the papers published by the institute for language in Sarajevo showed that this sort of standardisation began in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And has this -- has the standardisation been completed and, if so, when was it completed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Standardisation is a long process, especially when it comes to language, and it cannot be completed in such a short period of time. I therefore consider that it's still an ongoing process. The standardisation of the Bosnian or Bosniak language is still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That will be it for now. Well, just one -- one quick question. Back in -- on December 26, 1992, at the 182 session in the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we can seen in this courtroom before part of a transcript - it's under 1D 02663 - where there was a discussion at the time and where Izetbegovic was noting that a commission should be -- should be established in order to figure out what sort of name to give the Muslim language. Were you aware that these discussions were taking place at the Presidency level in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.
