And you spoke earlier about some intellectuals sometime around that period who had -- who had -- Muslim intellectuals who had been talking about adopting the name Bosnian or Bosniak or something to that effect, and earlier you told us that there was this commission that you had participated in, albeit up until April 1992, and I want to go back and again ask you when you were on this commission, did these intellectuals or this committee of intellectuals of Muslims, did they ever come up with a concrete proposal to name their language Bosnian or Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that this commission that I took as an illustration of what it was that we were doing did not go on for very long. There were one or two meetings. At these commissions there were no proposals for a name, so I don't know whether a name was provided in any official setting for the language of the Muslims, especially not Bosniak or Bosnian. In private conversations, though, of course I did hear things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let's go back to the work done by this commission. You told us that there were two meetings, and you were a member of the commission. Did you take part in the work done by this commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the name of the ministry and the Croatian cultural society Napredak, I worked on that commission. As far as I can remember, I have already referred to all the things that the commission discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course the commission that met twice tackled some issues but that was a long time ago. As far as I can remember, when the issue of the three languages was raised, Bosnian, Serbian, and Croatian, did the commission members, you included since you were part of it, did you deal with these issues -- this issue on the basis of the territory, or did you look at it from the perspective of the nations, the peoples? Let me take an example, a very specific one. In Croatia you had the Krajina region with Serbs in it. Did the commission look into the language used by Serbs in Croatia with the consequences that that might have entailed? So did you have to look it -- at it from the people's perspective, or did the commission only work on the territorial issue, as it were? So if you had the republic as an entity, was it possible for some to use the three languages regardless of the territory or regardless of the people? So in a nutshell, was the territorial issue the main drive behind the work of the commission, or did you just look into the fact that a Serb in Croatia could speak Serbian, or a Croat in Herzegovina could speak Croatian, or a Bosnian in Zenica could speak Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I noticed then and what I'm certain of, almost, is that none of the professors on that commission or beyond that commission ever spoke of any territorial reasons. So in this case we can talk about this subject matter from a purely scholarly point of view. However, those discussions would not lead us to speedy solutions, I believe, because scholars invariably quarrel over things like this. So in response to your question, there were no territorial reasons that would motivate the speakers to name the language on that basis. It was exclusively the right of every people to give the language their own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to be switching to another topic, and this deals mostly with regulations. Of course, the first two documents, let's go through the first one 1D 00199. 1D 0199. This is dated 9 December 1992 we see "a decree on secondary education in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during the imminent threat of war," and of course a couple of things that we might want to focus on. If we look at Article 75, for instance, dealing with financing of secondary education, it says: "Secondary education will be financed from the HZ HB budget; funds shall be issued to the account of the Secondary School Fund for the administrative body for the education of the HZ HB...." Now, before we go on to talk about the rest of the document, if you could tell us prior to the war, who funded secondary education? At what level was it funded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Secondary education was financed at the level of the republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, to your knowledge and understanding, did the state government or the republican government, whatever you want to call it at the time, did they come with any money to this area in order for the secondary -- the schools, you know --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But did they come at this particular time? In December did they come from Sarajevo to finance these schools? 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In 1992, December, we have this, and I'm wondering whether you could tell us if the government in Sarajevo was fulfilling its financial obligations to the secondary schools in this area by financing them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I said a few moments ago that that's what they did before the war. However, in 1992, the ministry from Sarajevo and the government had no contacts whatsoever with the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, outside Sarajevo itself, that is. The ministry in Sarajevo, from that point of view, was quite ineffective. There was no possibility for that kind of thing to be done. So the ministry from Sarajevo did not finance this -- or, rather, schools outside Sarajevo at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me go on to the next document and then I'll probably ask you a question that goes for both of them. 1D 00200. 1D 00200. This is again 9 December 1992, and this is a "decree on primary education in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And if we look at Article 7, for instance, it talks about the funds necessary to achieve "the needs and interests of society set out in Article 6 of this decree shall be allocated from the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and from municipal budgets." Again let me ask the same question that I asked with respect to secondary education. How about primary education prior to the war? Who was funding primary education in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Also the republican budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it just as with the secondary education, nobody from Sarajevo came to finance the primary education in this particular area at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to look at this last -- second to last Article, Article 82. Perhaps you could comment on this very briefly. It's at the last page. Article 82. It states: "When this decree enters into force of law on primary education (Official Gazette of the SR BH/Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina/ ...) shall cease to be valid." And again I want to ask you I guess a question that would go to both these two decrease, 1D 00199 and this one 1D 0200, if you could tell us why was it necessary under the circumstances to draft these decrees? Why couldn't the schools, elementary and secondary, simply continue to function as they had been just prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Quite simply for the reasons we've already referred to. The key thing regarding education, both secondary an elementary was the financing of it. So those who finance it have to be confirmed by regulations. So at that moment the ministry from Sarajevo had no possibility of doing that. Therefore, it was only logical that somebody else would have to do that, somebody who would pay for the education involved and finance it. In this case it is the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look for comparative purposes, because the whole issue of Croatisation has coming up. So if we could look at as an example, for instance, what was happening in Tuzla. Let's look at 1D 00235, and along with this I will be looking at the following documents as well with which is 1D 00236, but let's start with 1D 00235. December 1992. This is the 19th. That is 10 days, 10 days, after the decree that we just saw, the two decrees from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and this is a "Decision to take over the rights of Founder with regard to the School of Commerce RO/work organisation/ in Tuzla and transform it." Have you had a chance to look at this particular decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from this particular decision can you tell us what is happening? What is this decision all about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Actually, it is one and the same thing. The question is who the founder is going to be and who is going to finance what is going on in the school itself. That is to say, who is going to finance the teaching process. In this case, it is the town of Tuzla or the municipality of Tuzla that takes upon itself to become the founder. They also cannot communicate with the ministry so the ministry cannot carry out these obligations. Again it is the same situation that we saw in the case of HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just to make sure that I full I understand this and forgive me if I'm asking a silly question, but is this a new school that is being founded or is this one that already existed and now there's just the takeover of it, because by taking over now they take over the responsibilities of doing that which the State was incapable of doing, that is, financing it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: This is a school that already exists, and it is being transformed at the very same time. So these are two different things. It is being transformed, but it already does exist de jure and de facto.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we go to the next document, 1D 00236. Okay. Have you had a chance to -- this is a decision, 19 December, 1992. Again, ten days after the decrees from Herceg-Bosna. This is a "Decision to take over the rights of Founder with regard to the Secondary Electrical Engineering School Centre in Tuzla and transform it." Have you had a chance to look at this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, I have had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to sort of save some time, is this decision similar to the one that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It is the same pattern, the same reasons. So it is the municipality of Tuzla that takes upon itself to become the founder so that the school could function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And now I guess the question that needs to be asked. What is the difference between what Tuzla is doing ten days after what was being done by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object at this point. I think the witness is being asked to speculate on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if I -- I believe I've laid a foundation for the last hour and a half. The gentleman worked in the Ministry of Education. He's worked in various schools. He understands the system perhaps better than any one of us here, including those of us who have gone to schools in that area. So I think if anybody's qualified to give an answer is this particular gentleman. We're not asking him to speculate. What we're asking him is base on the text itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Professor, or Under-Secretary for Education, you've heard this question. Can you answer Mr. Karnavas's question without speculating, however? As long as you have enough knowledge to give a specific answer based on the knowledge you have of this very specific field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed this is the same thing. If we look at the text from a substantive point of view, the key thing in these two texts and in texts that have not been referred to, and there have been other cases of this kind, namely where the ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not meet its obligations, then the municipal structures of government would take upon themselves to become the founders so that the school curriculum and the school itself could function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. Now we're going to switch to another topic, and it primarily deals with schools but slightly different. So I'm going to first refer to a document on 1D 00438. This is -- we had talked about the names, and so I wanted to get that out of the way, so I put this at the very top of the pile, because you were asked some questions, especially from the Bench, with respect to one name, the name of the university. Here we have a decision dated 16 September 1992 on changing the names of a number of primary schools. So if we just look at the very first one. The Braca Simic primary school is called 1st Primary School Mostar. Now, could you -- and then we go down. 2nd Primary, 3rd Primary. We can see the names being changed. First of all, in changing the names to 1st, 2nd, 3rd Primary School, was that political in any way or would it be neutral?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: If we look at all of these names that we can see here, that is to say the names of the schools, then we will notice that certain schools -- or, rather, certain names are indifferent, ideologically speaking, whereas others have a strong ideological undertone. For example, the 25th of May is Tito's birthday. The 14th of February, again one of the dates. Then the name of Franjo Kluz is the name of a Communist combatant. Most of the names that appear here are actually -- actually have an ideological dimension or an ideological connotation. Some of these names, the Simic brothers, that is something different. There are writers here, Braca Simic, Svetozic Corovic, Hamza Humo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. I'm going to beg you to please listen to my question first and then we'll go step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So my question has to do with what the schools were changed to the names. We see 1st, 2nd, 3rd. They were changed. Now, calling a school the 1st Primary School of Mostar, is that -- is there any political connotation to that, ideological or national?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No. No. No. These names are quite indifferent from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, looking at the names, can you pick any of the names that are, say, Croat?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Braca Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: These are two renowned Croatian writers who hailed from Herzegovina. One of them is a great poet, and the other one was a great poet and critic. They lived in the beginning of the 20th century. Simic died in 1925 or thereabouts. His brother went on. He lived a lot longer. At any rate, ideologically from every conceivable point of view these persons are indifferent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But they're Croat.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Also Franjo Kluz is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The Ribar brothers are Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again let me just go step-by-step. It's important for me. It may not be for you. With Franjo Kluz, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Franjo Kluz was a Communist activist and he was a fighter, I think in the war. But anyway, he was a Communist activist at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next Croat that you see, who is he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Well, Franjo Kluz and then the Ribar brothers. The Ribar brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Who are they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Well, during the Second World War they were very well known as they cooperated with Josip Broz Tito. One of them was the president of the youth organisation, if we could put it that way. He was the leader of the youth. He was considered to be very revolutionary. I think he got killed in 1943 in an incident of suspicious nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not going to go through all the names but suffice it to say there is a list of not just Croat but also Muslim and Serb names that are being changed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, one last question with respect to this document. The names that were chosen for these particular schools, 1st Primary, 2nd, 3rd and what have you, how were they chosen, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: This has to do with Mostar and what I heard when I asked about it later. I think that it had to do with the previous names of the schools involved. Sometime in the 1970s these names were adopted, the ones that were being changed now. Instead of the existing ones that had been there earlier on, the 1st Elementary School, the 2nd Elementary School, these are names that had existed before the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we're going on to switch subjects a little slightly, still sticking with schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. We have a few questions. Witness, I just looked at this decision on the change of names taken by the Mostar HVO president, Mr. Topic. If I understand properly, before this decision was made, did the schools have names? For instance, the Braca Simic school? Does that mean that each school had a name, and the Mostar HVO changed all the school names? Did they do that in a neutral way by giving each school a number, 1st Primary School in Mostar, 2nd Primary School, and so on and so forth? Does this mean that well-known Croatian figures were removed, that also famous Communists' names were removed in order to make the schools absolutely neutral? Is that how this document should be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally, Your Honour, would interpret this document in a similar way to the way you've interpreted it. The names of the schools mentioned here had already existed until the 1970s in this neutral ideological sense. Then the sponsors of the new proposal that had to do with these new names, most of which were ideologically marked, well, they were simply replaced by the previous names. The HVO Mostar simply returned the old names that had been in existence in Mostar. At the same time, there was a de-ideologisation of the names concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand, after the Second World War, after 1945, was it so that the schools were numbered, and then in 1970, I suppose that was with Marshal Tito, he must have decided to change things by Croatising some schools. And then Mr. Topic, on the 16th of September, 1992, de-Croatised the schools. He returned to the previous system. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may say so -- well, you are not quite right in everything you've said. It is not Tito that had anything to do with the naming of schools. Even then it was done by the municipal authorities. However, in the 1970s it was done by the committee of the league of Communists of the Communist Party. In the post-war period the names of the schools mentioned here in Mostar were probably set as such so that there would not be an ethnic affiliation that was readily discernable. Since Mostar was a multi-ethnic city they simply wanted to avoid any king of connotations of this kind. However in the 1970s came the Communist ideologisation. At any rate, people who were members of the League of Communists, well, they had to be; and they were in agreement with the then district committee of the League of Communists, and they adopted this list of names where there are not only ideologically marked names but also a few names that were names of renowned writers who were relevant to Herzegovina and Mostar. As a matter of fact, the Simic brothers, Svetozar Corovic, Hamzo Humo, Osman Dzikic in actual fact were all people from Mostar. They were either born in Mostar or they were active in Mostar. Most of the other names are completely ideological from a Communist point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand. I didn't know that until 1970 there was this committee of the League of Communists which had changed the names, and now one understands better thanks to you what happen. But in 1970 one does see that there are two currents to Communists and the names are going to appear, and some famous Croat writers, but in 1970 was there no name of no famous Muslim which could be on the list of the names for schools? Was there none? Or Serbs, Serbians, names, Serbian names. Was there any? Was there none?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes, there were. The names listed here, the ones I've read out, are famous names in the literature of the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. If I may add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... we have here is there a Muslim name, a writer who -- who has been [indiscernible], or a Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Svetozar Corovic is a Serb. Hamza Humo is a Muslim. Osman Dzikic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there we are, very well. Very well. You have perfectly answered my question. I think my -- one of my colleagues had a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, witness. Mr. Karnavas, excuse me. Witness, about this document, 1D 00439 -- 38, sorry, 438, I did understand the system, I think, the former names for Muslim, Croatian, and Serbian names which were introduced around 1970 by the Communist League were replaced, and I find this system extremely intelligent to put these names, but I have two small questions to ask. The first is at the bottom of the list could you explain to me what is this new name, primary school Blagaj, and primary school Podvelez. At the bottom of the list, the last two lines. Of course I'm speaking of the English version. I don't know about the Croatian text or in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version there is a -- yes. The school previously called Omer Maksumic in Podvelez is now called the primary school in Podvelez. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So it was the name of the place which was kept, was it, local name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, yes. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's the name of the place. My second question now is that in the English text, second page, Article 2, last line I translate in French what I see: "The other primary schools keep their present name." Could you give me a few examples of the names which were kept and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, at this point in time I can't. I just don't remember that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think -- I think we -- we're clear on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But going back to that one question that was posed about Croatisation during the Tito years, would it be fair to say that there was no such thing -- there was no such tolerance on the part of Tito allowing any nation, let alone the Croat nation, of trying to Croatise any area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The term "Croatisation" is very strange to me. I understand it as a metaphor, but it might have a different significance in a court of law. I think one cannot apply it here. But with respect to your question concerning these names here, they do not have ethnic connotations. The names of the writers listed here have associations with a different context, a local context. These are people who are writers of the local Herzegovina area, not of a particular ethnic group, and that is why these names were used, not because they were Croats, Serbs, or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go to the next document, 1D 00600. 1D 00600. And I'm told that there may be an error, Your Honours, that you may not have this document. I don't know. If you don't, we can put it on the ELMO. Or e-court, sorry. Now, this is 25 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's 25 July 1992. I'm sorry. This is a "Decision on temporary form of certificates for final year of schooling." And of course if we look at Article 2, it does say that there will be a logo, the HZ HB logo, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and the exact title of the school shall be printed below the logo. My question is why was it necessary to passing such a decision at that time? Why couldn't they just simply issue certificates as they had been doing in the past?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: One of the reasons is the appearance of the form on which school reports are issued. In the middle of these forms there used to be a big five-pointed star and a coat of arms with factory chimneys, and in the heading it said "Socialist Republic." At that time these things caused negative reactions among people, and I think this was in fact the key reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right we go to the next document 1D 00620. It says 16 September 1992. This is on issuing diplomas by elementary and secondary schools. And if I were to ask you why was this necessary, I take it you would give me the same answer. You had the big star there representing an old system that had now been replaced, a system that evoked strong memories and emotions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document, 1D 00627, 16 September 1992. This is a decision to prohibit political activity in economic, social, and military organisations. And if we go to Article 1 it says: "Any form of political activity is hereby prohibited in educational, cultural, religious and economic organisations, civic associations and military units because political activity is not envisaged in their programmes and scope of activities." Now, some may understand why you do not want that in military units, but given that you no longer have a socialist Communist system, why not have political activities in schools and what have you? Why is there need for such a decision? If you know, please explain.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: This sort of decision, in my view, is well thought out. The prohibition of such activities in school, which would be educational rather than ideological institutions, is quite understandable. This decision adopted in an area where there was constant combat activity because Mostar and other areas of Herzegovina that were affected by artillery fire coming from the hills was intended to prevent politicking, and it was quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: It's quite logical and expected, and in my view well thought out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00683. This is December 16, 1992. This is a decision to cover temporary -- to cover transportation costs, to cover transportation costs. And it talks about monthly passes for daily teachers, professors and students in Mostar municipality for travel from their places of residence to the given educational institution. Why was this necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: At that time the -- well, people were poor, had no money. Transport had to be provided. It had to be -- it had to be subsidized or paid in full, and this was traditional and had been traditional even previously. Even before the war, transportation for schoolchildren and students was subsidized by the municipality. This also refers to students [Realtime transcript read in error, "witness"] traveling to Siroki Brijeg in this case. They had had rights even before this as they do throughout Europe to reduce the fares, and this was intended to help students and their parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in the transcript it says witness travel. We're talking about student travel. Student travel to Siroki Brijeg. That's where the exams were taken if I understood your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter said students.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Student travel and travel for professors going to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in Siroki Brijeg that's where the exams were given at one point. Is that why they're having to travel, or was -- were classes also being held in Siroki Brijeg until you moved to Neum?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In June, on the 25th of June, after the liberation of Mostar, at the first meeting at the university it was agreed that exams should be held in Mostar for those students who were in Mostar and in Siroki Brijeg for those who came from other places other than Mostar and that classes for the first and second year should be organised there. That's why professors and some students going to lectures had to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00744. This is a document that's dated 1 April 1993, although I see at the preamble above it says 1 April 1992. At the bottom it's signed as 1 April 1993. This is a decision to support the report of the commissioner for education. Have you had a chance to look at this document, and can you please tell us exactly if you -- if you know, what is this about, this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes. This refers to April 1993. As classes in Mostar in primary and secondly schools could not be organised because of frequent artillery fire on the town and the school year was drawing to a close, the normal school year, the one that had been envisioned and only two and a half months were left in the school year, it was requested that the headmasters of schools should provide safe premises for pupils and students and that they should be there, the teachers should be there; and it was up to the parents to decide whether and when they would send their children to those classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00751, this is dated 15 April 1993, and this is a decision on school terms in the elementary and secondary schools for the academic year, and it says 1992/1993, and we see if we look at Article I the first term is from 7 May 1993. The second term shall end -- I'm sorry, the first term ends on 7 May. The second term ends on 11 June, and the third term ends on 16 July 1993. Why was this decision necessary under the circumstances, if you know? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The regular school year consists of four trimesters. Those are three-month periods, and in this case, the president of the government who is proposing this decision in this brief time that is left from the 15th of April, 1993, to the 16th of July the same year, is trying to organise in a systematic way these trimesters in which classes should be held so that the pupils could move on to the next academic year. This is the structure of normal school year which has here been reduced to the days that are left in the -- from the month of April to the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally in this batch of documents 1D 01499. Again if we could -- this is for comparative purposes. This document is 13 August 1993, on or about the same period of some of the documents that we've seen thereafter. This is an order from a Dr. Safet Cibo, and it's the Jablanica municipality Assembly War Presidency. Can you please explain to us what is this order about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Jablanica was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time. In Jablanica there was a large number of refugees and a large number of school-age children. The -- whoever proposed this decision is asking for something similar to what was organised in Mostar, for classes to be organised in the period of time envisioned here in this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to the war who would be issuing such an order? Where would it be coming from? Would this be at the municipal level, regional level, or at the republic level?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: This sort of order would be issued by the ministry in Sarajevo before the war. It would come from the competent republican organ in charge of primary and secondary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In the period of time in question, as in the case of Tuzla and other places, the ministry in Sarajevo was isolated. Sarajevo was encircled. There was no communication, and there was no possibilities of financing these schools. So the issue was who could provide the logistics and organise the classes and cover the costs of this educational process, pay the teachers their salaries and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. One final question before we probably will have to take the break, but you had indicated to us that you had worked at the ministry in Sarajevo. During this period of time, granted Sarajevo was encircled, it was cut off, but did the Ministry of Education dispatch any of its colleagues, any of your colleagues, any members of the ministry of education, to go around the country to come, say, in Mostar with any orders, any instructions, any resources on how to finance these programmes, any certificates? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I only know that in the summer of 1994, as late as that, Mira Merlo, a sales servant from the ministry left Sarajevo and she visited some schools in Konjic and some other places, maybe in Jablanica. She found my wife's telephone number, my wife was a refugee, and told her that she had left Sarajevo. And I met her. She was staying with some relatives at the seaside. And that was my only contact with someone who was directly in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it the answer is no. Up until 1994, nobody came during this period. We're talking 1993, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Nobody came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I guess one -- it begs one more question because we know that around that time internationals were there, some international organisations such as the United Nations and other NGOs. Did they by any chance come around with resources, a printing press so you could print certificates, money so you could fund the education, costs for the transportation, proposals for a new educational curriculum? Did any internationals come to provide any such assistance to your understanding? I'm talking 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Nobody offered that kind of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it if it had been offered would you have accepted it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Certainly. We would have been very happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are just going to break for 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's about on to another topic, going back to the changing of the name streets just very quickly just to get this over with. If we look at 1D 00439. This is already in as an exhibit. It's a decision on the change of the names of the streets; and we see from Article I it says priority, the names of the streets in Mostar with Yugoslavian and ideological meaning will be changed. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we go to the next document, 1D 0440. Again, this is already in as an exhibit, but these are background questions. Now, this is decision on the appointing of a commission for the change of names of streets in Mostar. This is 6 November 1992. Do you see this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now I want to show you this document, which is not an exhibit yet, 1D 00662. This is 20 November 1992, and this is a decision on the establishment of a commission to name and rename streets and squares in Mostar municipality. And, sir, I'm going to ask you if you could look at Article I, Roman numeral I, and see of the nine names if you can identify any Muslim names on this commission and, if so, please point them out.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic is one. He is the vice-president of the commission. Kerim Cisic, a member of the commission. Nijaz Berhamovic, a member of the commission. I think Zlatko Udovicic, a member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And that concludes that section, and then finally I just want to go to the very last chapter which deals with university -- the University of Mostar. And the first document I want to show you is 1D 02804. And we can see it's dated 21 August 1993, and it says here: "List of employees who wish to continue their work at the University of Mostar." Now, at this particular time, 21 August 1993, were you employed at all in any capacity with the University of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: As I have already said, all the professors who had links to the university and wanted to work got together at the university in June after the liberation of Mostar and decided that in September the examinations would begin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Professor Palameta. I still try to find the previous document which -- which Mr. Karnavas has introduced as 662, but I do not find 662 but only 612. So I wonder if it was meant that the document 612, which is the [B/C/S spoken], et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not it. It's 1D 00662, and we can -- it should be in the e-court system. And I can provide, if Madam Usher wishes to come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this document, we're in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Karnavas for the interruption. Your Honour, the question that was posed is that this document, which is going to be shown to the witness, dates from 21 August 1993. If Mr. Karnavas could perhaps just clear that up, because I'm not too certain whether that's accurate looking at -- that it emanates from a stamp while all the signatures which appear on this document are dated in 1992. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, going back to what I was -- my previous question, you were answering it, I believe, at the time, and you indicated -- I asked you whether you were associated in any way with the university in Mostar, and I believe you were in the process of answering that question, but to cut to the quick, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's just look at number 1, for instance. We see the name.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see the faculty. We see the address, and then we see a date, then we see a signature. So we have the dates.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here we have 23 November 1992, and we have a signature. Could you please explain the dates and the signature.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The first date which we see in the stamp signifies that the document was verified and prepared for signing. The signing began on the 23rd of November when per number one Berislav Crnjac from Mostar an assistant lecturer at the faculty of civil engineering entered his details in the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what was the purpose of this -- of this list? I mean, we can read the title, but if you could help us out a little bit. What was the purpose of making this list?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The intention of this list was to obtain information showing how many staff members the university would have at its disposal for the beginning of classes in autumn. That's one thing. And the second reason was as it was still a war zone, everybody had some sort of assignment, so that expressing their wish to continue working at the university they were able to free themselves of other duties, whether military or otherwise, that they had been assigned. Those are the two main reasons. Quite simply to see what staff the university had at its disposal and for the people who wanted to work at the university to be able to be released from other obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, have you had a chance before coming here to go through the list and to look at the names and to see, at least as of the date of the signature that we see on the far right corner, how many Muslims are -- Muslim names do you find in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In this document there are about 90 or more Muslim names, about 15 Serbian names. Most of the professors who were Serbs had left Mostar. Several Jewish names, and a certain number of Croatian names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, have you had a chance to identify the numbers, because we see at the far left each name has a number. Do you have the particular numbers of those you believe are Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you now. Number 4, number 5, number 8, number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about number 10?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, number 10 also. And number 9 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to go through this --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Number 19. I can't see the numbers very well, but, for example, 41, 42, 43, 44, 46, 47, 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I think we get the point. I don't think that we need to -- unless the Trial Chamber wishes to have every single name or number read out, we can move on to the next document. I think we've made the point. Do you know, by any chance, whether all these individuals continued to work at the university throughout this period, that is, after November or December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I don't think they all continued to work at the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know if anyone was dismissed as a result of being of a particular nationality? I mean, in other words, that was the criteria?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I can assert that no one was dismissed as a result of being of a particular nationality. I don't think anyone was actually dismissed from the university in that period of time, at least I'm not aware of anyone being dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what if a particular professor failed to show up? In other words, he signed, he wanted to continue, but then simply didn't show up for weeks or months at a time. Would that person continue to be on the list, continue to receive a salary, continue to tie up a post which he was not taking advantage of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: For a while that person would continue to be on the list and on the payroll. If he didn't come to collect his salary, then the salary was not paid out. There was no one to pay it to. But when classes began, somebody had to teach, but no one was dismissed from their duty in six months. I can't recall any such instance. I don't remember anyone losing their right to be employed at the university. None of the professors. All the professors who turned up later and who contacted the university later on in 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, even if they were not on this list were taken back, and they were reappointed to the post they had held before the war. I'm not aware of anyone being rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, P 00714. P 00714. This is a decree on establishment of the work of University of Mostar during war or imminent threat of war, and I believe it's November 6, 1992. And of course if we look at Article 2.4, it says: "The language used at the university shall be Croatian." And I believe we answered that question, have we not? Or do you want --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again -- but I just want to make sure I'm crystal clear. When it says that the language shall be Croatian, is this a new language or is it the same language but just a different name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The Croatian language is a very old language. Croatian literature goes back to the early Middle Ages. That is when the name of the Croatian language began to be used. There was no new language called the Croatian language. If you are referring to the language taught in schools, then in this period the same textbooks, the same grammar books that had been used before continued in use. For example, the Babic grammar, which was used in schools even before the war throughout all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me go about it another way. The language that says here shall be Croatian, prior to November 6, 1992, what was it called? And I'm talking about in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: According to the constitution of 1974, the language is called Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, incidentally, this -- the University of Mostar, who was funding it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you -- let me withdraw that question and ask another question instead. Prior to the war, who was financing the university that was now called University of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: The fund, the republican fund at the ministry. So it was the republic which financed the work of all the universities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and all institutions of higher education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at Article 30 in this particular document, Article 30, it says, "Financing." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It says: "Funds for the work of the university shall be provided from the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the revenue earns through the university's own operations and other sources of funding in accordance with the valid regulation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Can you please explain to us why is it that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is now undertaking the funding of the university at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: For the simple reason that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at that point in time was the only entity able to finance the university. It issued this decree. There was no other source of funding. The republican fund was simply not functioning at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I failed to ask you a question earlier. I asked you about the professors being -- whether any of them were dismissed. Can you please tell us whether any students were turned away because of nationality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No. That never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at Article 31 it says here: "This Decree shall enter into force immediately, and it shall be applicable during the state of war, or until the socio-political organisation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been finalised and its legal system established." Now, let me ask a foundational question. Were you aware of this document at the time, that is, when you were involved with the university and then when you were also at the same time, as I understand it, the deputy head of office for education -- or department of education, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, how do you explain Article 31? What do you understand it to mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Like all the decrees pertaining to education, this one also was provisional. All the decrees issued at the time were provisional until the authorities were normalized and communications established, as happened in 1994. In every case it was always thought that agreements would be reached on Bosnia-Herzegovina as the common state of all the three peoples living in it and that it was simply a question of time, and as soon as the war was over things would take that course. No decision issued by the university, and I have never seen any other decision by any other organ in Bosnia-Herzegovina which did not include Bosnia-Herzegovina in its heading. The stamp of the university, all the university documents bear that name. In this decree, it had to be a decree because it was temporary, it was provisional, and it was replaced by the law on the university later on, and this -- this was then a permanent law, not a provisional one. And always it's pointed out that this is provisional until the system of Bosnia-Herzegovina is established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we look at 1D 02115. This is February 26, 1993, and it says -- it's a conclusion. Under number 1 it says: "Consent is given for the organisation of an educational process for the first year." Under number 2 we see that some money totaling 60.000 DM, I take it that means Deutschmark, equivalent in HRD, which I would take to mean the Croatian dinar. And then if we go to number 5, which is probably what is most important it says: "Students coming from families of killed members of the Armed Forces HZ HB are exempt from paying the participation fees contained in item 4 of these Conclusions." I guess my question to you is, first, what is this document about; and secondly, number 5, does this mean that only Croats or members of the HVO, students coming from families where -- of killed members of the HVO are exempt? How do you interpret number 5, and how, more importantly, was it applicable at the time -- was applied at the time, enforced?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Allow me first to answer the first question you put. This document refers to the organising of classes in Neum. It's very important to know why classes were organised in Neum. We've already explained that because it was impossible to reach the university in Mostar safely, exams and classes were relocated to Siroki Brijeg. Siroki Brijeg, however, did not have the elementary requirements for students to stay there, attend lectures, for teachers to stay there. There was no restaurant or canteen there, for example. And even had there been, it would have had to have been paid for. So one of the main reasons was to move to Neum -- that was one of the main reasons why the move to Neum was made, where there were hotels and where both local and visiting professors could stay and conduct the classes in peace. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina approved certain funds to pay the hotels for accommodation, food, and other expenses, and in the decree it says that students had to pay 50 marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. You said the government -- the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina approved certain funds. So are we saying Sarajevo approved these funds?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean -- I didn't mean that. I meant Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And please slow down so that the translators don't make any mistakes as a result of your speed. So you're the contributing factor of this, so slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Thank you. The answer to your second question concerning the exemption of students having to pay these 50 German marks and it says in Article 5 -- or paragraph 5 that these are students coming from families of killed members of the armed forces of HZ HB. The HVO was the only formation at that time which was legitimate -- the legitimate armed force in the area, to the best of my recollection, and HVO units had among their members not only Croats but also Muslims and some Serbs as well. So all those who had this right and also in similar cases they were really able to enjoy this right. But in practice anyone who did not have money, they didn't have to come from a family of a killed member of the armed forces. Nobody even raised this issue with the student if they were unable to pay whoever the student was. No one was sent back from Neum because they did not have 50 German marks. That's my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 02802. This is dated 15 October 1997, and it's a decision, and we see that it says, Article 1: "At her ... request, Djulsa Bajramovic ends her employment by consent as of 9 May 1993." Now, before I ask I my question let's look at the next document, which is 1D 02801. We see a decision on giving consent to term 1998 employment. Article 1: "Consent is hereby given for the undisputed termination of employment of Djulsa Bajramovic at the Faculty of Education of the University of Mostar as of 9 May 1993." And again we can see that dated 31 October, 1997. So could you explain to us if you know how these decisions came about, and how can somebody consent to terminate their employment in 1993 some four years later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I have seen a few such documents, and I wondered what this was about. The answer was that persons who continued working at the faculty after May 1993 did not have those years of service recognised by the retirement and pension fund. They had to actually terminate their work relationship before the Muslim-Croat or Croat-Muslim conflict in order to regulate this. That was the explanation that was provided to me and that I'm providing to you now. So in such cases deans would try to accommodate the employees involved, and then the rector would verify the decision and you can see that on another document. You can see a signature. Quite simply they tried to accommodate people who had had that kind of problem. Now, how they regulated the matter altogether that is something I don't know. It's probably the retirement fund that could give you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, from looking at the name can you tell us whether this was a Croat, Serb, or Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A let me ask you one final question. Do you know whether this particular individual worked after this? I know we see that this is a consent for termination, but did they work after this period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: She submitted her request in 1997. She had already retired. She had retired earlier on. In order to regulate her pension - that's what they explained to me - she had to ask for the termination of her employment to be ante-dated. So the date of the 9th of May, 1993, was placed here. So it's a four-year difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I guess my question is did she work -- did this particular person -- I know that they wanted, for whatever reasons, 9 May 1993 to show that the person stopped working at the university, but my question is very concrete. Do you know for a fact whether this particular individual worked after May 9, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I cannot really give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 00421. And we see that this -- do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: This is actually a photocopy from a book that was published to commemorate 100 years of university education in Mostar. So these are two pages from the text that was then written by the then-rector, Franjo Ljubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And have you had a chance to look at this document and to see whether the information that is conveyed in this document is -- is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I remember having reviewed the document now and having read it earlier on. There is nothing that would be contrary to the truth to the best of my knowledge. I believe that the information contained in this document is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't want to go through the entire two pages, but let me just focus your attention to the part of the text where it refers to footnote 9. That may help you locate the text. And let me just read part of it. It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this would be, Your Honours, on the second page. After the title page, that is, on the left-hand side, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "In the beginning of the academic year 1992, 1993, the name and the official language were changed. The majority of professors, associates, workers, and students of the Bosniak, Jewish, Serb, and other nationalities supported the decision. They continued to work and study at the university. A great number of professors, non-Croats, during and after the war have been deans," and then it lists the names of the particular deans. And at the faculty level as vice-rectorate and at the university senate? Then if we look at footnote 9, it does say: "Only few professors of the Bosniak national, former Muslims, disapproved the introduction of the new official language (but not the name of the university). They did not want to participate in the educational process, discouraging students from the university. It seemed odd that such an event happened in October 1992, six months before the Croat-Muslim conflict broke out and two years before the establishment of the Bosniak language. As a major group -- as a minor group, they were not able to persuade other professors and associates (non-Croats) not to take part in the education process. They could not make students not to enroll and study at the university." And I guess my question now is, sir, is how accurate is this, and if you could please elaborate a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Obviously Rector Ljubic knew who had reacted. I personally had not heard any reactions to that effect from any professor with regard to language. I did not hear of any such thing. Rector Ljubic, who was a professor at the time, probably knew these things better and certainly had more information about this. His statement that the number is very small speaks in support of that. So it is not a big number. Also, I do not know about cases of them trying to talk students out of doing this. I cannot say. Rector Ljubic would know that better than me. However, perhaps I didn't pay enough attention to the footnote. In general terms, it does seem logical to me on the basis of the elements that I was aware of and that I had heard of from other people. No one complained to me personally in respect of such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, sir. I want to -- I appreciate your testimony. I have no further questions at this time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in relation to this last document I have one small ancillary question to ask. I'm a bit like Diogenes, who was walking in Athens in full daylight with a lamp and people were asking him what are you doing and he said, "I'm looking for the human nature." So without these documents I'm trying to find the truth about these documents and to know exactly what happened in order to really understand the situation. So in this document which deals with 2.000 -- 1992 to 2002, I discover out of the blue, I didn't know, that April 7, 1992, apparently Serbs shelled the student housing as well as the faculty of economics, and in this document we see that Major Momcilo Perisic, over Radio Mostar, announced that these two building had been shelled. And we discover that he made this announcement because five pilots were kidnapped or would have been kidnapped. So this is of course very marginal compared to this document, but I would like to know whether you were aware of this event, because when someone announces that a faculty building and a student housing building is going to be shelled, that's not peanuts, you know. And when we discover the cause, when we look, General Perisic seems to say that it is because some pilots had been kidnap. Had you heard about this event that these -- at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this sentence of this general of the Yugoslav army had become a very well-known thing. Everyone working at the university had become aware of it precisely because of its cruelty. No one could have expected this kind of statement to be made. When it was broadcast, it didn't cross anyone's mind that it would actually be carried out. I wasn't in Mostar at the time, but I know how my colleagues reacted. Indeed there was firing. As for the five military persons that he is speaking about, to this day no one knows who the said persons were. Quite simply this was a threat that had to be motivated by something in this broadcast. Namely they -- it is there, and it remains as an image of what was going on in Mostar. That wasn't the case only then. The faculty was shelled and civilian buildings too. That went on for years. That was the reason why the faculty moved and why the schools didn't start working. I cannot give you any more details in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this answer to my question. Let's now see what we have in store for cross-examination. We have questions? I've consulted with my fellow Judges, and we had assessed that an hour should be enough for all other Defence teams, but who will -- who is going to ask questions? I see General Praljak on his feet. Mrs. Nozica, any questions on your Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Stojic's Defence team will have no questions, although it is not my turn; but I think that Mr. Ibrisimovic would be the first, so I think that we should go by the right order for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ibrisimovic. I think I understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then who's next? No questions for Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about General Petkovic? Mrs. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Petkovic's Defence will have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic for General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Praljak informed me during the break that he would have a very brief question that came to his mind during the examination. We didn't manage to discuss it at any length, so I suggest that you allow him to put the question and you will assess how relevant it is. I assume it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well with. In order -- in order not to have no problems, this is in line with his competence; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite frankly, I did not fully understand it, but the general told me that he only needed two or three questions very simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. Yes. Quite simply as someone who was at the academy for theatre, film, and television, and who was taught by Dr. Bratoljub Klaic, one the greatest experts in this field when I studied language and literature, and since we talked about language earlier on, and this is a topic that probably reemerge, and the professor gives me a good opportunity to put four questions over five minutes it won't go on very long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Professor, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You heard that it is language and this problem that it is going -- that is going to re-emerge in this court time and again but I have the following questions four. Do you know the following names: Marin Drzic, Petar Hektorovic, Petar Zoranic, Marko Marulic, and Semata Relkovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, I know these names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do we consider them to be the classics of Croatian literature?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, particularly the first ones you referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So Drzic, Hektorovic, Zoranic, Marulic; right? In the order that I enumerated them, they wrote so many works. For example, Dundo Maroje, Ribanje i Ribarsko Prigovaranje by Hektorovic; Planine, the first Croatian novel by Petar Zoranic; Judita by Marko Marulic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. These are Croatian Renaissance authors from the 15th and 16th centuries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, my last question -- or, rather, the one but last. Tell me, highly educated persons in Croatia who did not study Croatian literature or the literature of the Yugoslav peoples, when they read these works can they understand them in their original form?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure. In order to understand any one of these authors, it is hard to provide an answer in the affirmative, namely that a person could understand. One had to know the language that was spoken at the time in Dubrovnik and the language in which Drzic wrote in. Then the Language of Split, Cakovica, written by Marulic or Zoranic, other authors. So no comment -- or, rather, without any comments provided it would be hard to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: As you studied literature, do you know whether an English person can understand Shakespeare without any problem, and can a Frenchman understand Cornee and Racine without any problem?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV PALAMETA
utterances.text: I'm not sure they would understand Shakespeare or Milton as readily as they would understand contemporary authors. So without comments again you couldn't understand a text like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, well, we have other Englishmen here who we could ask some other time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Of course when the time comes I'm going use this as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now time to adjourn -- almost time to adjourn, actually. I believe that Mr. Karnavas used up two hours and 40 minutes, but the registrar will give us the exact count. On Wednesday we're sitting in the morning, and we will start with the cross-examination by the Prosecution. I believe Mr. Kruger will be in charge of the cross-examination. Is that it, Mr. Kruger?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, Mr. Kruger, you've got a whole day to get ready, an entire day to get ready, and I'm sure that way you'll be able to really prepare. You're very lucky. So we'll meet again on Wednesday, 9.00 a.m. Have a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of October, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
